frase_gancho.texto: An impossible body turned into a clay vessel.

puente_narrativo.texto: Move on to the next display case: a tiny face just eight centimeters tall, half living face and half skull. The same village, now speaking of death.

guion_corto.texto: This gray clay vessel is the Acrobat of Tlatilco. A man rests his chest, elbows and chin on the ground and bends his legs back until his feet touch his head. The mouth of the vessel is on one of his knees. Look at the details: a short loincloth, hair parted down the middle, pierced ears and filed teeth. It appeared in a tomb, that of a man of about forty years old, accompanied by thirty-one luxury objects. A fairground performer? Researchers prefer to think of a ritual specialist, who twisted his body to enter a trance. It is more than three thousand years old, and it still seems to be having fun.

guion_largo.texto:
Tlatilco means, in Nahuatl, “place where there are hidden things,” and the name suits it perfectly. This village, on the shore of the ancient Lake Texcoco, in what is today Naucalpan, lay hidden beneath the earth for more than three thousand years. Until, in the 1930s and 1940s, workers at some brickyards began to dig out clay and, along with the clay, figurines, vessels and bones. The artist Miguel Covarrubias understood what they had in their hands and alerted the archaeologists. Since then, hundreds of tombs have been explored.

Imagine what the village was like. Houses of wooden poles and mud with thatched roofs, fields of corn, beans, squash, chili and cotton, fishing and hunting on the lake, and two domestic animals, the dog and the turkey. There were already people who devoted themselves only to making ceramics, people who brought stones from far away, and people who healed. The village was growing, and with it the variety of trades and ranks.

Its inhabitants buried their dead beneath the floors of their houses. For them, the ancestors remained part of the family: they slept beneath the living. That is why we know so much about Tlatilco today: each tomb was a time capsule, with ornaments, vessels and figurines.

The Acrobat came from one of those tombs, number one hundred fifty-four. There lay a man between forty and forty-five years old, with filed teeth just like the figure on the vessel, and with him thirty-one prestige objects. Some came from very far away: jadeite, a green stone that does not occur in the Valley of Mexico, as well as hematite, quartz, obsidian and bitumen. In other words, this gentleman had connections. His tomb tells us that someone in Tlatilco was connected to a world much larger than his village.

Now think about the design. It is a bottle, a container for liquids, and the ingenuity lies in the fact that the figure is the container: the mouth, where it is filled and emptied, is a knee. There are several contortionists in the art of Tlatilco, and there is debate about what they were. Fairground performers? Healers? Practitioners of a rite? For many researchers they are religious specialists, people who with their bodies opened a door to the world of the spirits. Bending until your feet touch your head demands dedication and discipline, and whoever managed it held a special power.

If you went through Hall 1, you may remember the skulls with filed teeth and the modeled heads. Here you see the same custom turned into a portrait: in Tlatilco the body was decorated and transformed, with filed teeth, carefully styled hair and red paint, traces of which still remain on the vessel.

One last observation for when you return to the display case. The artist who made this vessel thought of everything: the balance of a body that barely rests on three points, the knee turned into a neck, the carefully parted hair, the loincloth marked with fine lines. It is not an improvised object: it is the work of someone who knew his craft very well and took it very seriously.

And the idea of a body that twists or flies to touch the sky does not end here. Centuries later, upstairs, in the Sierra de Puebla hall, you will see the costume of the Voladores (Flyers), who launch themselves into the air from a very tall pole. Different eras, the same desire: to use the body as a bridge to the sacred.

texto: Find the mouth of the vessel: it is on one of the knees
Look at the filed teeth and the pierced ears
Find the traces of red paint on the gray clay

texto.Culture: Preclassic of the Central Highlands / Basin of Mexico
texto.Dimensions: 25 cm high x 16 cm wide x 20 cm long

texto.pregunta: Myth: The Acrobat was a circus or fairground performer from the village.
texto.respuesta: Reality: It is a funerary vessel that appeared in a tomb; researchers think it more likely represents a ritual specialist in a trance, although no one can be certain.
